frontier.hypothesis: The 4-insn head residual is decided in reorg.c's fill_simple_delay_slots, not in sched: our blez's delay slot is filled from BEFORE the branch (the addiu a2,sp,1040 that sched2 leaves last in the block) while the target's is filled from the FALL-THROUGH thread (move t4,zero). A C form that makes the last pre-branch insn ineligible for the slot - the target has an mflo there, and reorg cannot hoist an mflo into a delay slot - restores the target's rows 54-71 in one step.
frontier.mechanism: reorg.c's fill_simple_delay_slots scans backwards from the branch for an independent insn in the same basic block and only falls through to the branch target / fall-through thread when it finds none. Our block ends ... mflo t3, addiu a2,sp,1040, blez; the target's ends ... addiu a2 (row 54), mflo t3, blez. So the question is not which order sched2 emits (s17 measured those equal) but which insn is LAST before the branch.
frontier.next_probe: Dump .dbr and .sched2 for the incumbent (pwsh tools/grinder/dump.ps1 func_8003DE14) and read the head block's insn chain immediately before jump_insn 96 in both - confirming that addiu a2 sits last pre-reorg and that reorg moved it. Then look for C forms that place the dst cursor's materialisation earlier in the block's dependence order, e.g. giving dst a use inside the head region, or making the total = rect[2]*rect[3] multiply the last thing computed before the guard, so that the mflo is the final pre-branch insn. Score each with sandbox --disable all.

frontier.hypothesis: g_src's allocno priority can only be lifted through its live RANGE, not its schedule: with the pick order proven equal to the target's, the remaining levers are the NUMBER of g_src references (nrefs >= 15 at livelen <= 13 gives pri >= 35000) or an earlier last reference (livelen <= 10 gives pri 36000). Both are decided before sched1 by where the g-channel value is read.
frontier.mechanism: global.c prices an allocno at nrefs * 10000 * something / livelen; s14 derived the exact arithmetic (px pri 32727 at nrefs 12 / livelen 11, g_src pri 30000). s17 removes the schedule from the set of things that can move livelen, so only the C-level reference pattern remains.
frontier.next_probe: Use tmp/grind/func_8003DE14/s16/batch_alloc.py to read nrefs and livelen for g_src directly (not inferred from the score) over a family of forms that vary ONLY how many times the g-channel source value is read and where its last read sits - e.g. folding the g sum's second operand through g_src, or deriving a later value from g_src instead of from px. Reject any form whose alloc table shows px's priority moving too, since s16 measured that steering the seat re-prices the arm.

frontier.hypothesis: The b_src / $v0 conflict-set difference (s16 frontier item 2) is now the only remaining RA lever with an untested mechanism: the target's $v0 is free of global allocnos because b_src is excluded from it by a conflict our build does not have.
frontier.mechanism: global.c hands each allocno the lowest-numbered free hard register that does not conflict. b_src (p128, pri 32727) takes $v0 in our build, so it conflicts with nothing there; the target seats b_src on $a0, meaning $v0 was unavailable at that point - a flow.c liveness question, a different lever from priority arithmetic, and one s17's scheduler result does not touch.
frontier.next_probe: Dump .flow/.lreg conflict information for p128 on the incumbent (tmp/grind/func_8003DE14/s16/d_base) and identify which live range would have to overlap b_src to exclude $v0; then search the already-banked s16/carrier_alloc.json corpus for spellings in which b_src is seated on $a0 while px, g_src and r_src keep the incumbent's priorities, and score those with sandbox --disable all.
